speakers: Niels Kaastro Larsen (host, Top Traders Unplugged)
summary: Niels Kaastro Larsen and Alan Dunne (August 2026) cover the US yen intervention, Fed credibility under Warsh, rising US yields, and August trend-following results. Dunne's 'three fractures' (sticky inflation, debt sustainability and fiscal dominance, institutional erosion) imply bonds are a weaker equity diversifier, and trend has earned most in stress periods this decade. They also compare AQR and GMO capital market assumptions and argue trend remains competitive when cash rates are 3.5-4%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: it is very rare for the uh the the US to intervene in currency markets they intervene I think in 2011 but the last time they they bought the Japanese yen was back in 1998.
claims.claim: In late July 2026 the US intervened in the yen, selling euro and buying yen, the first yen purchase since 1998, and said Japan could tap the Fed's FIMA facility to borrow dollars for further intervention.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: sensitivity the US has to a big uh bond holder selling bonds at the moment and the sensitivity they have to rising yields
claims.claim: The intervention reveals US sensitivity to Japan selling Treasuries and to rising yields, with a reluctance to let a big holder sell, consistent with a heightened concern about the bond market.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the Fed cut rates and dollar yen had a huge collapse in about 4 days.
claims.claim: In the 1998 episode intervention first stabilised the yen but then Fed cuts triggered a massive carry unwind in USDJPY within four days, so pushing currencies one way risks second-order instability.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: Japan has actually turned out to become really the the the only place the US can go to get some of their military stuff built
claims.claim: There are industrial-policy motives: Japan has become the main place the US can get military equipment built in time, so yen policy is about more than currency levels.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: the price had a initially a decent move, but some of it has obviously um uh disappeared again
claims.claim: The yen intervention's effect partly reversed shortly afterwards.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: both of which actually went against the the bigger trend. Um so that would have hurt performance.
claims.claim: In August 2026 the yen intervention and the US bond-market 'intervention' (Bessent's announcement) went against the prevailing trends and hurt trend followers.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: notably seeing good gains on the commodity side in August
claims.claim: August 2026: US yields flat to lower, outside-US yields slightly higher, and managers showed good gains in commodities.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: from the perspective of the role of trend in a portfolio and and getting diversification you know it's always a very encouraging sign when you see stronger trends in the commodity markets.
claims.claim: Strong commodity trends are a key diversification benefit of trend because most investors cannot access commodities successfully themselves.
claims.indicator: commodity trends (zinc, wheat, lean hogs, copper)

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: So they were both kind of a weaker dollar trade which would have been negative for for trend followers.
claims.claim: The dollar sell-off after the bond intervention (with gold up) created a weaker-dollar reversal that hurt trend followers while currencies were choppy.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you see some people trading in credit for example and that was a negative uh others with kind of non-trend signals doing a bit
claims.claim: Dispersion among CTAs in July 2026 arose from idiosyncrasies: credit trading hurt, non-trend signals helped.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: some some managers not trading the full set of exact asset classes others trading a very narrow set.
claims.claim: Large dispersion among CTA ETFs comes from different asset-class coverage, and buyers often do not know what is behind the product.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: we see the Btop 50 up 2.14%. In August, up 10.26% so far this year.
claims.claim: August 2026 (to 25 Aug): Beta50 +2.14% (YTD 10.26%), SG CTA +1.34%, SG Trend +1.19%, Short-Term Traders +1.69%, MSCI World +2.68%, S&P 500 TR +2.58%, US Agg bonds +0.78%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: normalizing the balance sheet um which would obviously increase the supply of bonds in the market at a time when the treasury is uh trying to uh you know increase its demand and reduce its supply of bonds
claims.claim: Fed chair Warsh blames QE for deficits, but shrinking the balance sheet would add bond supply while Treasury shifts issuance to bills, so large balance-sheet reduction is unlikely soon.
claims.conditions: No framework yet; task forces pending

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I'm kind of a bit skeptical that we're going to see much in the way of balance sheet reduction um in the short term
claims.claim: Alan expects little balance-sheet reduction near term, since the Fed chair speaks regularly with the president and has not given a framework.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: about the degradation in short-term trend following in um in some contracts, but not all.
claims.claim: A CFM-associated paper found a degradation of short-term trend performance in some contracts, which has been known for a while.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the size of the CT industry relative to the liquidity of the futures market is not so so large that there is a is a concern around that.
claims.claim: The paper rejected industry size as the explanation for weaker trend performance; CTA assets are small relative to futures liquidity, so medium/long-term trend is not overcrowded.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: having that fast reactivity having that convexity um that you get particularly in in kind of as you go into riskoff periods.
claims.claim: Short-term trend is kept for fast reactivity and convexity going into risk-off periods.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: when I see short-term managers managing even two three four plus billion dollars. I'm really curious how do the how do they do that successfully without it becoming just way too expensive to to execute.
claims.claim: Short-term strategies have capacity limits: managers with several billion dollars face execution costs, and AUM inflows after good narratives often precede lost returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: all the managers I know in the short-term space they're not really trend followers. They're like V expansion type strategies or whatever.
claims.claim: Many managers described as short-term trend are really volatility-expansion strategies.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: I think on fixed income trend positioning is probably in line with the macro narrative the trend is for higher yields for all the reasons people are worried about
claims.claim: CTA fixed-income positioning (short, for higher yields) matches the macro narrative, while the dollar narrative (pessimistic) conflicts with CTAs' net long dollar exposure.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: it's completely crazy to pay any attention uh to these to these um things in my opinion
claims.claim: Sell-side notes estimating CTA flows (e.g. buy $70bn equities if the S&P closes above a level) should be ignored because much more goes into CTA positioning.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: at certain times even though you're quote unquote a longerterm manager we can change positioning pretty quickly.
claims.claim: Longer-term trend managers can cut exposure quickly (e.g. in the yen after intervention), so positioning narratives are unreliable.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the market doesn't have a sense on the Fed's what's called reaction functions and how they're seeing the economy
claims.claim: Warsh's reduced guidance leaves the market without a sense of the Fed's reaction function, which is the problem rather than forward guidance itself.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: you know at the moment we've got this uh AI boom it's inflationary in the short term it may be disinflationary down the line
claims.claim: The AI boom may be inflationary short term and disinflationary later, which complicates what policy is appropriate and how the Fed will respond.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Wall Street has always tried to infer what the Fed was doing you know even before the 1990s when they um didn't even make an announcement
claims.claim: Markets have always inferred the Fed's stance (liquidity matters), so telling markets to ignore the Fed makes no sense.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the curve steepened you know the dollar sold off gold rose all of these classic signs of of uh reduced uh credibility
claims.claim: After the July FOMC press conference the curve steepened, the dollar fell and gold rose: classic signs of reduced Fed credibility, as the Fed has missed its inflation target for five years.
claims.direction: steeper curve, weaker dollar, gold up
claims.conditions: Fed fails to back words with action

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: possible uh fracture within the Fed that you could get kind of distinct um factions.
claims.claim: Three FOMC members favour raising rates, increasing the influence of Waller and Williams and raising the chance of factions within a politicised Fed.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: my own view is is I'm shifting to the view yet maybe he is more dovish than than he's letting on and he doesn't want to raise rates.
claims.claim: Alan suspects Warsh is more dovish than he signals.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: out that you know um growth is strong um strongish you know not make it strong and inflation has been above target for for quite a while.
claims.claim: Yardeni/Druckenmiller-type argument: with decent growth and inflation above target, the 10-year yield near 5% is not unusual.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: we're just normalizing back to where they were in the 1990s and the 2000s and the 2010s was the aberration.
claims.claim: Yields near 5% are a normalization to the 1990s-2000s; the 2010s was the anomaly.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the size of the debt is much greater now. So the debt service cost is is greater.
claims.claim: Higher debt means rising debt-service costs as low-yield debt rolls off and issuance shifts short, adding pressure against raising rates.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: what's pushing up yields is uh real yields which reflects greater competition for capital because, you know, governments have greater deficits and we've got this huge capex spend related to AI.
claims.claim: Yield increases come from real yields (inflation expectations steady at 2.25-2.5%), reflecting competition for capital from deficits and AI capex.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: inflation being higher and stickier which we've seen and obviously the upshot of that is um you know basically the bonds and equities become more correlated
claims.claim: First fracture of the regime-adaptive paper: higher, stickier inflation makes stocks and bonds more correlated (contrasting with the disinflationary Great Moderation era).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: saw it in 2023 when there was concerns about US debt issuance and then the change to the quarterly refunding.
claims.claim: Debt sustainability scares recur (2023 issuance fears led Yellen to change refunding; now Bessent is tinkering), showing officials intervene when yields spike.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if you had you know an equity market um decline the US economy is so levered in the US uh equity market at the moment that would have you know a meaningful impact on on on debt
claims.claim: Second fracture: high debt with high equity valuations means an equity decline would worsen debt (recessions ratchet debt up), potentially tipping into fiscal dominance as debt/GDP exceeds 100%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: financial repression and that's basically holding down interest rates below where they should be uh to try and manage debt service levels
claims.claim: Financial repression (holding rates below where they should be to manage debt service) is the related risk, visible in Bessent's actions.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the fraying institutional order or the the erosion of institutional norms.
claims.claim: Third fracture: erosion of institutional norms (pressure on the Fed, active tinkering in bond issuance, fading fiscal conservatism).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: the debt concerns also mean that you know bonds you know would would be less reliable diversifiers for equities too.
claims.claim: Both sticky inflation and debt concerns make bonds less reliable diversifiers for equities, with significant asset-allocation implications.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: as soon as you get a sense that that that the US is heading towards these kind of policies you see it in the dollar h you see it in gold you see it in bitcoin
claims.claim: Financial repression and fiscal dominance are positive for gold and bitcoin and show up in the dollar.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: part of the challenge that trend followers were facing in the 2010s was a high degree of uh coordinated and successful um policies by central banks
claims.claim: In the 2010s coordinated, successful central bank policies produced low, stable rates and inflation, a headwind for trend following.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: stock gen trend has annualized nearly 7 and a half% over this decade to date where it was just under 2% in the previous decade
claims.claim: This decade (to August 2026) SG Trend annualised nearly 7.5% versus just under 2% in the 2010s, while US bonds went from +7% to negative and equities from 13.5% to over 15%.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: bond equity correlation now it's um positive 0.3 this decade uh versus last decade it was negative 0.5.
claims.claim: Stock-bond correlation moved from -0.5 last decade to +0.3 this decade.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: bonds and trend were positively correlated last uh decade 0.33 whereas this this decade bonds and trend are negatively correlated negative 0.37.
claims.claim: Trend flipped from +0.33 correlation with bonds last decade to -0.37 this decade, and from +0.2 with equities to -0.16.
claims.indicator: trend correlation to bonds and equities

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: between April and October of that year bonds were down 20% uh and trend was up 9% equities was only up three
claims.claim: In the 2023 bond sell-off (April-October) bonds lost 20%, trend gained 9%, equities only 3%, when debt concerns peaked and Yellen shifted issuance away from long bonds.
claims.direction: trend up when bonds sell off

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: some of the the best periods of performance for trend have been when we've seen these uh fractures that I'm talking about when we've seen them really start to bite in the market.
claims.claim: Trend's gains this decade concentrated in 2021-2022 (inflation, bonds and equities falling together), 2023, and the last 12-15 months (debasement trade, metals), when the regime fractures bit.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: outside of that it's generally been in periods when bonds have been doing badly and not when equities have been doing badly.
claims.claim: Trend this decade has earned money when bonds did badly rather than when equities did badly (2022 aside).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Its ability to capitalize on new themes emerging in markets like that sustainability wasn't a theme in markets in the last decade.
claims.claim: Trend's adaptive nature lets it capture new market themes such as debt sustainability, which was not a theme last decade.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: interspersed with kind of periods that looked more like the old regime.
claims.claim: The sticky-inflation regime was interspersed with disinflationary episodes (immaculate disinflation, AI hopes), so it is not constant.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: when we got up close to the highs, they they came out with the announcement and we we've seen that kind of playbook
claims.claim: Treasury acts when 10-year yields approach 5% (as in October 2023); a decisive break above could be the straw for equities and a strong environment for trend.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: at some point if you did see that yield uh break and and we see a ratcheting higher in yields, would that be the straw that breaks the camel's back for for the equity market?
claims.claim: A ratcheting rise in yields could break the equity market, the scenario where trend shows portfolio benefit.
claims.direction: equities down if yields break higher

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: a strong period for trend uh in a period where equity returns have been strong.
claims.claim: Trend does not need an equity crisis to make money; it was strong this decade alongside strong equity returns.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: namely the commodities have done really well and at different times which uh has been very uh useful
claims.claim: Commodities have done well at different times this decade, a useful contribution to trend.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: The correlation between markets are not as high as it used to be within the sectors and and and that's generally good for for trend
claims.claim: Within-sector correlations seem lower, partly from deglobalisation and US policy, which is good for trend (anecdotal).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: One is you can look at the past uh and say, well, what is what have equities done over the long term? Or else you can build in some kind of uh yield uh version.
claims.claim: Capital market assumptions are built either from long-term historical returns or from starting yields.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: if the 10-year yield is, you know, 5%. Then that's a pretty good proxy for what you can expect to receive uh if you bought a bond and held it for maturity
claims.claim: For bonds, the starting 10-year yield is a good proxy for the 10-year return.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: earnings yield in the US which is the inverse of the price earnings ratio uh and based on a certain assumption about earnings growth and inflation
claims.claim: Equity return forecasts use the earnings yield plus assumptions about growth and inflation; equities have more moving parts.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: in AQR's uh analysis US equities are priced to deliver um about 3.9% real over the next uh you know 5 to 10 years uh and that's a nominal return of 6.3%.
claims.claim: AQR forecasts US equity returns of about 3.9% real (6.3% nominal) over 5-10 years, assuming unchanged valuations.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: But in a normal interest rate environment, they're forecasting a negative real return of 7.2% negative 7.2% for US large.
claims.claim: GMO forecasts a real return of -7.2% for US large caps in a normal rate environment, because it assumes valuations and profit margins mean-revert.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: something that's supposed to be kind of you know nearly scientific in approach can yield such massively different outcomes.
claims.claim: Capital market assumption exercises give radically different answers depending on assumptions (valuation mean reversion vs unchanged), so should be treated with caution.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: they basically take the long run average return of an equally weighted basket of commodity futures and according to their analysis that generates a a 3% geometric return over cash
claims.claim: AQR estimates an equal-weighted commodity futures basket earns about 3% geometric over cash (about 6.8% nominal).

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: really pessimistic on on say trend following and you're going to say it's going to be uh you know a 0.1 sharp a at 12 all I mean that's still a you know that's still a 5% return
claims.claim: With cash at 3.5-4%, even a 0.1 Sharpe trend strategy at 12% volatility yields about 5%, and 0.3 Sharpe over 7%, so trend is competitive on expected return.
claims.indicator: trend expected return vs cash rate

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: from a portfolio context again it begs the question why don't we see much higher allocation
claims.claim: Trend's low or negative correlation to bonds and equities begs the question why allocations remain low.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: okay equities are going to deliver 7% % but really they believed the equities were going to deliver 12 to 15% because that's the way it's been for the last while.
claims.claim: People forecast 7% equity returns while believing in 12-15% because of recent history, which distorts allocation.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: is that actually the higher the interest rates go the the more you benefit as well because we simply don't use that much of the cash.
claims.claim: Trend funds use little cash so the interest income largely returns to investors; replacing some bonds with trend costs little interest income.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: those periods of negative to flat to negative for the S for the 6040 have all come after periods of extre exceptionally strong returns.
claims.claim: GMO's lost-decade chart shows flat or negative 60/40 decades followed exceptionally strong periods, as the last decade was.

claims.speaker: Alan Dunne
claims.quote: Now we're seeing debt sustainability becoming a a new theme, you know, and then at some point does it infect the equity market?
claims.claim: The regime theme moved from inflation to debt sustainability; the next question is whether it spreads to equities.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastro Larsen
claims.quote: we're simply not going to buy anything that's going down, for example.
claims.claim: Trend helps with timing: it avoids buying falling assets and being early, which is key because being a few years early on a view loses investor confidence.
